entry.title: Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1589
entry.content:
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.

Key holding: Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

entry.title: Jason Perry v Australian Port Service (Qld) Pty Ltd Trading AS Ausport Marine [2026] FWC 4146
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission resolved a s.739 dispute concerning the Ausport Marine enterprise agreement, principally the date for the first CPI wage increase and travel-time/reimbursement entitlements under cl 12(a). The Deputy President issued a recommendation answering five questions and confirmed that s.739 cannot be used to terminate the Agreement or revisit the BOOT.

Key holding: Clause 12(a) entitles an employee to reimbursement for kilometres and tolls only where the employer requires the employee to use their own vehicle, not where the employee chooses to do so.

Therefore, in my view, the entitlement to be reimbursed for distance travelled and tolls is limited to circumstances where the use of the employee's own vehicle is a requirement by the employer, not a choice by the employee.

entry.title: Doran Herrick v Bupa Aged Care Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4141
entry.content:
In [2026] FWC 4141, Mr Herrick lodged an unfair dismissal application after his May 2025 dismissal from Bupa Aged Care Australia Pty Ltd, despite having signed an Employee Separation Agreement containing release and bar-to-proceedings clauses. The Fair Work Commission found the agreement constituted a binding settlement, declined a stay, and dismissed the application under s 587(1)(c).

Key holding: A binding settlement or accord and satisfaction extinguishes the existing cause of action and replaces it with a new cause based on the agreement, so an unfair dismissal application barred by an executed separation agreement has no reasonable prospects of success.

In Australian Postal Corporation v Gorman1, Besanko J held that the existence of a binding settlement or 'accord and satisfaction' extinguishes the existing cause of action and replaces it with a new cause of action based on the agreement. That is the case in the matter before me.

entry.title: Charles Patterson v P.A.P. Heating Solutions Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4135
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered an unfair dismissal application by Mr Patterson against a small business employer, PAP Heating. The dismissal was for alleged performance issues, but the employer’s written warning did not state that dismissal was at risk and the employer terminated before a promised meeting. The Commission found the dismissal unfair and awarded compensation.

Key holding: To satisfy the “Other dismissal” limb of the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code, a small business employer must expressly warn the employee that dismissal is at risk if performance does not improve, not merely that further action may follow.

However, the warning did not say that Mr Pa tterson was at risk of being dismissed if there was no improvement. As a result, the dismissal was not consistent with the Small Business Code.

entry.title: Thomas McGuire v Woolworths Group Limited [2026] FWC 4140
entry.content:
Thomas McGuire was dismissed by Woolworths Group Limited on 8 August 2026 and filed an unfair dismissal application on 8 September 2026, outside the 21-day period. He sought an extension of time under s 394(2) of the Fair Work Act 2009. The Fair Work Commission refused the extension because it was not satisfied that exceptional circumstances existed under s 394(3).

Key holding: Mere ignorance of the Commission’s unfair dismissal jurisdiction or the 21-day time limit is not a sufficient basis for granting an extension of time under s 394(3).

Mere ignorance of the law is not a sufficient basis for the grant of additional time.

entry.title: Application by Abdul Samee Paracha [2026] FWC 4142
entry.content:
Mr Paracha applied under s 536LU of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair deactivation remedy after his Uber driver account was deactivated on 25 September 2024. The Fair Work Commission amended the respondent name to Rasier Pacific Pty Ltd and dismissed the application because Mr Paracha was not a person protected from unfair deactivation. His pre-commencement platform work could not be counted, leaving only about one month of relevant service.

Key holding: Under s 536LD(c), a platform worker must have performed work on a regular basis for at least six months at the time of deactivation to be protected from unfair deactivation.

Because Mr Paracha has not performed work on a regular basis for a period of at least 6 months, he is not a person protected from unfair deactivation.

entry.title: Ryan Anderson v Coles Supermarkets Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3086
entry.content:
Mr Anderson, a long-serving casual Coles team member, was dismissed after restraining a suspected shoplifter at an adjoining Liquorland and later attending the Coles store while suspended. The Fair Work Commission found a valid reason based on the 1 December 2025 safety-policy breach, but held the dismissal harsh and unreasonable due to his long service, clean record, isolated conduct and lack of deliberate breach. The Commission considered compensation appropriate.

Key holding: A dismissal with a valid reason may still be harsh and unreasonable where the seriousness of the conduct is outweighed by relevant matters under s 387(h), such as long service, a good record and an isolated, non-deliberate breach.

entry.title: Julie Winship v HACCP International Property Services Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4048
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission found that HACCP International Property Services Pty Ltd unfairly dismissed casual cleaner Ms Julie Winship after raising vague performance concerns, removing her shifts and failing to provide particulars or a real opportunity to respond. The employer did not file materials or attend the hearing, and the Commission proceeded on Ms Winship’s evidence. Compensation was ordered under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth).

Key holding: A dismissal is unfair where the employer cannot establish a valid reason and fails to give the employee proper notification and a real opportunity to respond to alleged unsatisfactory performance.

There was no valid reason for HACCP to dismiss Ms Winship.

entry.title: Mr Adrian Clay v Peninsula Directional Drilling Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4077
entry.content:
In [2026] FWC 4077, the Fair Work Commission considered a jurisdictional objection to Mr Adrian Clay’s unfair dismissal application against Peninsula Directional Drilling Pty Ltd. Mr Clay was General Manager with guaranteed annual earnings of $235,000, above the high-income threshold, and the Commission found he was not covered by the Clerks—Private Sector Award 2020 because his principal purpose was managing the business, not clerical work. The unfair dismissal application was dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

Key holding: Coverage under the Clerks—Private Sector Award 2020 requires the employee to be wholly or principally engaged in clerical work; incidental clerical duties do not establish coverage where the principal purpose of the role is management.

Having regard to the evidence of the duties and responsibilities of the work performed by Mr Clay, the extent to which he engaged in any clerical work as defined in the Award, was incidental. While I accept that some of the work performed by Mr Clay was clerical in nature, I am satisfied that he was not wholly or principally engaged in clerical work.

entry.title: Mining and Energy Union (301V) v Anglo Coal (Moranbah North Management) Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4109
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission arbitrated a dispute under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) over a Level 2 written warning issued to Mr Jamieson for arriving late and failing to seek approval for altered hours. The Commission found substantial procedural non-compliance with the employer’s misconduct policy and the Agreement’s fair, transparent and measured requirement. The extract provided does not include the final order disposing of the warning.

Key holding: Where an enterprise agreement obliges an employer to apply disciplinary procedures fairly, transparently and in a measured way, a substantial failure to put the specific misconduct allegation and afford a genuine opportunity to respond means misconduct is not confirmed under the policy and disciplinary action is inconsistent with the agreement.

However, a s the requirements of cl 6 were not wholly or substantially met, misconduct in the workplace was not confirmed under cl 6, and so Appendix A was not enlivened. Accordingly, it was not, in my view, consistent with the policy to take disciplinary action.

entry.title: Ms Judith Bruce v Community Based Support Limited [2026] FWC 4076
entry.content:
Ms Bruce applied under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) alleging unfair dismissal by Community Based Support Limited. The employer objected that the dismissal was a genuine redundancy after it ceased NDIS services. The Fair Work Commission held the role was redundant but the employer failed to comply with enterprise agreement consultation obligations, so the objection was dismissed.

Key holding: An enterprise agreement obligation to consult by “discussion” requires more than inviting written feedback; it requires a real two-way exchange about the likely effects of the change.

Clause 7 of the Agreement requires a "discussion" - something more than simply the identification of an issue upon which input or "feedback" is then sought.

entry.title: Mr Josateki Vunimasi & Mr Aminio Cava and Others v Woodward Foods Australia Pty Ltd & Mr Richard Tomasevic [2026] FWCFB 284
entry.content:
This was a Full Bench appeal concerning seven PALM scheme workers whose s 365 general protections dismissal applications named Woodward Foods as respondent, although their actual employer/dismisser was Whales. The Deputy President found no valid s 365 application because they did not allege dismissal in contravention of Part 3-1, and the Full Bench refused permission to appeal. The appeal also sought to raise joint employment and host-employer oral promise arguments not argued at first instance.

Key holding: For a valid s 365 application, the person must have been dismissed and must allege that the dismissal contravened Part 3-1; otherwise the Commission’s s 368 powers are not enlivened.

It is abundantly clear that the Deputy President applied the principle outlined in Milford. He properly determined that the Appellants were not entitled to make applications under s 365 and nor were the functions of the Commission under s 368 enlivened because the second criterion was not met.

entry.title: Kawicki v Trustees of the Marist Brothers t/as Marist Brothers Sydney Province [2026] NSWCA 220
entry.content:
The appellant, a former student, sued the Trustees of the Marist Brothers for damages arising from sexual abuse by Brother Florentine; the primary judge awarded $186,000 but declined damages for diminished earning capacity. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal against the refusal of past economic loss, with Adamson JA dissenting. The appeal concerned only economic loss; liability for the sexual abuse and the $186,000 award were not in issue.

Key holding: A claimant alleging past economic loss from historical abuse bears the onus of proving that the abuse caused a diminution in earning capacity productive of actual financial loss; a tribunal may reject the claim by not being satisfied, without making a positive finding of no diminution.

A failure to be satisfied that there was a diminution in earning capacity is different from a finding that there was no diminution in earning capacity. The onus to establish a diminution in earning capacity rested on Mr Kawicki.

entry.title: Harvey v State of Queensland [2026] QCA 214
entry.content:
The Queensland Court of Appeal dismissed Mr Harvey’s appeal from a decision refusing to set aside his notice of discontinuance of a police assault damages claim filed more than seven years earlier. The Court found no error in the primary judge’s discretionary conclusion that the appellant had not shown good reason, or that the interests of justice required, setting aside the discontinuance, given unparticularised evidence and unexplained delay.

Key holding: Even if a court may set aside a notice of discontinuance where the interests of justice require it, unparticularised claims of duress or mental illness and lengthy unexplained delay will not satisfy that test.

Assuming in the appellant's favour that the court had power to set aside the discontinuance if it was shown to be in the interests of justice to do so, the material before the primary judge did not satisfy that test.

entry.title: Lamont v The Royal Women's Hospital (No 4) [2026] VSC 687
entry.content:
In the principal negligence proceeding, after judgment was reserved, the plaintiff applied to defer delivery of judgment pending a possible application to reopen based on four documents. The defendants sought costs against the plaintiff’s solicitors, Shine Lawyers. The Supreme Court of Victoria found the deferral application was an abuse of process and ordered Shine Lawyers to pay both defendants’ costs on an indemnity basis.

Key holding: A court may make a personal indemnity costs order against a solicitor where the solicitor advances an application that is an abuse of process and lacking in merit, in breach of the solicitor’s duty to the Court.

In circumstances in which I have concluded that the deferral application was both an abuse of process and lacking in merit, and that Shine Lawyers acted in a way that was in breach of its duty to the Court, I am satisfied that an order for indemnity costs should be made.

entry.title: Phan and Australian Skills Quality Authority [2026] ARTA 2457
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed ASQA’s decision to cancel Mr Phan’s CPC31320 Certificate III in Wall and Floor Tiling, obtained through RPL from the deregistered RTO Kingsway. It found reasonable grounds that Kingsway did not provide or arrange the necessary RPL assessment and declined to exercise its discretion not to cancel. The reviewable decision was affirmed.

entry.title: Mr Johnathon Burr v The Trustee for Cornerstone Labour Hire Unit Trust [2026] FWC 4121
entry.content:
Mr Burr’s host assignment with CEVA Logistics ended and he brought an unfair dismissal application against his labour-hire employer, Cornerstone. The Commission had to decide whether Cornerstone dismissed him or whether only his host placement ended; because Cornerstone kept him on its books and sought alternative work, the application was dismissed.

Key holding: Where a labour-hire employee’s host placement ends but the labour-hire employer remains ready and actively attempts to redeploy the employee, the employment has not been terminated on the employer’s initiative and there is no dismissal under s 386(1).

Under s 386(1), a person is considered dismissed if their employment with the employer has been terminated on the employer's initiative. It follows that if the employment continues or if the employer is actively seeking to find alternative work for the employee, there has been no dismissal.

entry.content:

entry.content:
The ETU brought a s 739 dispute against Ausgrid over whether Leading Hands performing Emergency Response Coordinator (ERC) on-call duties in Newcastle/Lower Hunter should be paid higher duties at Level 1 of the D2 Field Supervisor band. The Commission found ERC work overlapped with the Leading Hand role and was not the work of a higher-band Field Supervisor, so clause 13 did not apply. It declined to dismiss for want of a live dispute but answered the formulated question “no”.

Key holding: A Leading Hand performing ERC duties is not entitled to higher duties pay under clause 13 because ERC work overlaps with and is contemplated by the Leading Hand role rather than being the responsibilities and duties of a higher-band Field Supervisor Role.

For the reasons set out above, I am not persuaded that the work performed by an ERC is to be regarded as that of a Field Supervisor and not that of a Leading Hand. Rather, I accept Mr Richardson's evidence that there is an overlap between the Roles when it comes to emergency response, and that such overlap is a feature of the R&P Framework.

entry.title: Ms Belinda Turton v Suncare Community Services Ltd [2026] FWC 4084
entry.content:
Belinda Turton applied for an unfair dismissal remedy against Suncare Community Services Ltd. Suncare applied under s 399A of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) to dismiss the proceeding for non-compliance, relying on Ms Turton’s failure to attend a staff conciliation and a directions hearing. Deputy President Butler refused the non-compliance application.

Key holding: A conciliation conference conducted by FWC staff is not a conference conducted by the FWC for the purposes of s 399A(1)(a).

I do not consider a conciliation conference conducted by the staff of the FWC to be a conference conducted by the FWC for the purposes of s 399A(1)(a) of the Fair Work Act.

entry.title: Mr Gabriel Roccisano v Chop Shop Post Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4091
entry.content:
Mr Roccisano applied under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy after being notified of his dismissal by Chop Shop Post Pty Ltd on 4 November 2025. His application, filed on 12 December 2025, was out of time on either possible calculation of the end date. Deputy President Butler refused to extend time, finding that the medical evidence did not establish incapacity to lodge and that distress, financial pressure and ignorance of the 21-day limit were not exceptional circumstances.

Key holding: For the purposes of s 394(3), the distress inherent in losing a job is not of itself an exceptional circumstance, and neither is an asserted psychological condition exceptional unless it is shown to have incapacitated the applicant from lodging within time.

As the cause of action is founded on something as inherently distressing as job loss, distress per se cannot be considered exceptional.

entry.title: Ying Pang v Newpoint Consultant Pty. Ltd. [2026] FWC 4101
entry.content:
This case concerns an application under s 365 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) by Ms Ying Pang alleging a general protections dismissal by Newpoint Consultant Pty Ltd. The Commission found the employment relationship ended on 30 June 2026 and that the application was filed three weeks late, and refused an extension of time because exceptional circumstances were not established.

Key holding: The Commission cannot extend time for a late s 365 general protections application unless satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist having regard to the s 366(2) factors.

Because I am not satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances in connection with the late filing of the application, I cannot allow additional time for the application to be made.

entry.title: Application by The Australian Workers' Union (002N) & The Australian Licenced Aircraft Engineers Association (107N) [2026] FWC 4057
entry.content:
The Australian Workers' Union and the Australian Licenced Aircraft Engineers Association applied under s.459(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) to extend the 30-day period for protected industrial action authorised by a protected action ballot declared on 30 September 2026. The employer did not object but asked that the extension be limited to 14 days because the unions had earlier agreed not to commence industrial action before 14 October 2026. The Fair Work Commission granted a full 30-day extension.

Key holding: Under s.459(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Fair Work Commission has a discretion to extend the 30-day protected action period by up to 30 days, and there is no statutory presumption as to the length of any extension.

As the length of the extension, I accept that the Commission has a discretion to grant a period up to 30 days. There is also no presumption about that length in the Act.

entry.title: Ms Vikki Turner v Ithaca Crystals Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4080
entry.content:
Ms Turner lodged an unfair dismissal application under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). Her former employer asserted she was not protected because it was a small business and she had not completed the minimum employment period. Ms Turner sought to amend to a general protections claim under s 586 (with an alternative extension of time under s 366(2)); the Commission held the application was in substance a general protections claim filed on the wrong form and allowed the amendment.

Key holding: Although s 586 cannot be used merely to substitute a general protections cause of action for an unfair dismissal claim so as to avoid ss 725/729, the Commission may waive the irregularity and permit amendment where the initiating application was in substance a general protections claim made on the wrong approved form.

Though there is no power to amend an application to substitute a general protections cause of action for an unfair dismissal one, that does not mean that the form in which the application is made is determinative. If a party simply uses the wrong form to make one type of claim or the other, that is an irregularity that can be corrected or waived pursuant to s 586 of the Fair Work Act: Hambridge v Spotless Facilities Services Pty Ltd

entry.title: Stephanie Tranquille v New Beginnings Network [2026] FWC 4103
entry.content:
New Beginnings Network sought that Commissioner Durham recuse herself from determining its s 603 application to vary a $5,025.00 compensation order made in favour of Ms Stephanie Tranquille, alleging apprehended bias arising from case management rulings, a conciliation conference and the Commissioner's conduct of the hearing. The Commissioner heard the recusal question herself on the papers and refused it. The substantive variation application remains outstanding, with the original compliance date of 22 October 2026 unaffected.

Key holding: A Commission member should not lightly accede to a recusal application, and apprehended bias is not established unless the applicant identifies the matter said to deflect the decision-maker from the merits and articulates the logical connection between that matter and the feared departure from impartial decision-making.

It is clear from the authorities to which I have referred that I should not lightly agree to recuse myself. New Beginnings have not provided substantial grounds to warrant me doing so.
